name: Self-Sustaining Hype Cycle
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: How Four Different Loops Combine Into One Unstoppable Looking Machine
lesson.summary: The hype reinforcement loop, sunk cost escalation loop, career incentive loop, and geopolitical arms race loop are not just parallel, they actively feed each other, producing a hype cycle that can sustain itself for years without matching technical progress.
lesson.body:
Each loop feeding a hype cycle has its own separate logic. The hype reinforcement loop runs through media coverage, startup valuations, and stock prices, each of which rises partly because the others are rising. The sunk cost escalation loop runs through institutions that have already committed billions of dollars or years of political capital to a technology, and who find it easier to fund one more round than to publicly admit the earlier rounds may not pay off. The geopolitical arms race loop runs through national governments funding quantum research out of fear that a rival nation will gain a strategic or economic advantage first, a fear that only grows once a rival government announces its own funding increase. And the career incentive loop, covered in the previous chapter, runs through the individual scientists, students, and advisors whose livelihoods depend on the field staying fashionable.

What makes a hype cycle self sustaining is that these four loops do not just run in parallel, they reinforce one another. A national quantum initiative announcement is itself a geopolitical arms race move, but it also generates press coverage that feeds the hype reinforcement loop, which helps startups raise the next funding round, which lets universities create more funded PhD positions, which strengthens the career incentive loop, which produces more optimistically framed papers, which generates more press coverage, which puts political pressure on the next government to increase its own funding so as not to fall behind. Follow that chain far enough and it becomes circular. Each loop's output becomes another loop's input.

Consider a concrete, simplified version of one pass through the cycle. A government announces a large quantum computing investment, framed around the risk of losing a technological race. Financial press covers the announcement, and venture capital funding for quantum startups increases in response, since investors read government commitment as a signal of eventual commercial payoff. Universities respond to the larger funding pool by expanding graduate programs in the area. More graduate students and postdocs, all needing publishable, fundable results, increase the volume of upbeat papers and conference talks. That volume of activity becomes evidence, cited in the next round of press coverage and the next government's budget request, that the field is moving fast and must be kept up with. No single actor orchestrated this. It emerged from each part of the system doing what its own local incentives rewarded.

The dangerous property of a self sustaining cycle like this is that a lack of genuine technical breakthroughs does not necessarily slow it down, because political fear, sunk financial commitments, and career needs each have their own independent momentum that does not require validation from the underlying science to keep turning. That raises an obvious and practical question, which the next chapter takes on directly: if a system like this resists correction from within, where, if anywhere, can it actually be interrupted?
